title: Bonhoeffer's end (1945)
hook: executed weeks before liberation; his prison letters still read worldwide

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bonhoeffer's book and his warning. Your line was not cheap grace. Did you take a step toward the costly good thing, or just look at it? Either counts. Day nine hundred fifty.

Prisoner Bonhoeffer, get ready to come with us. That, by one account, is what the guards said, at the door of a schoolroom where a group of prisoners was being held near the end of the war. The pastor had just led a short Sunday service for the others. He took a book, wrote his name in it, and asked one of the men, a British officer, to carry a message to a friend in England if he could. Then he went with the guards. The officer remembered the message. Today, the end of Dietrich Bonhoeffer's life, and the words he left behind.

Bonhoeffer was arrested at his parents' house in Berlin and held for a long time in a military prison. Through family and friends, he had become connected to people who were plotting against Hitler, and after a failed attempt on Hitler's life, those connections were uncovered. Christians still talk about this honestly. A man who wrote about following Jesus and was drawn toward peace joined, in some way, a conspiracy to kill a tyrant. Some see it as costly obedience in an impossible time. Others hold it as a hard question that doesn't resolve. In prison, he wrote. Letters to his parents, to his fiancée, Maria, and to his closest friend, Eberhard Bethge, who later gathered them into a book. They're full of ordinary things, a request for books, thanks for a parcel, and full of big questions about God and faith in a world that seemed to go on without either. He also wrote poems. In one he asks who he really is: the calm man the guards see, or the restless one he knows inside, and ends by placing the question with God. Near the end he was moved to the concentration camp at Flossenbürg and hanged there, shortly before the war in Europe ended. The message the British officer carried was short. As he remembered it, Bonhoeffer said: this is the end, for me the beginning of life. That echoes an old Christian hope, which Paul puts this way in the King James Bible: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" The letters are still read today. People who share none of his faith read them too, for the honesty.
screen: `WHO AM I? A QUESTION GIVEN TO GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write to someone you won't see soon. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is far away, by distance, by time, or by a falling-out. A grandparent. An old friend. A cousin overseas. Bonhoeffer's letters mixed small news with big things. So start a letter in your head with something ordinary: what you ate, what you're reading. Then add one sentence that matters, the thing you'd want them to know if this were your last letter. If you pray, you can hold them before God as you write. The bell holds the time.
Bonhoeffer's end. A pastor executed by the Nazi state, who left behind prison letters and, by one account, called his death the beginning of life.
Your line: the beginning of life. Today, send the letter, or a message, to the person you pictured: something ordinary, and one sentence that matters. Day nine hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Bonhoeffer is remembered on the calendars of several churches, including Lutheran and Anglican ones, and his prison letters and poems are read in study groups, sermons and private devotion.

notes: Claims rule: no dates (arrest 1943, execution 9 April 1945) and no count of weeks before liberation. 'Shortly before the war in Europe ended' stands in.

Hook: the guards' words, the schoolroom at Schönberg, the Sunday service, the book with his name, and the message to Bishop George Bell all come from Payne Best's account; the guards' words are paraphrased without quotation marks (Best's 1950 book is under copyright).
Last words paraphrased as remembered by Payne Best ('This is the end, for me the beginning of life'); framed 'by one account'.
His involvement in the conspiracy through the Abwehr (Hans von Dohnanyi) is described generally; the two readings are given without ranking. Confirm the framing.
The poem 'Who am I?' is paraphrased only.
Listed on Lutheran and Anglican calendars: confirm the howItsDone wording.
